transcripts.title: Interview 05
transcripts.text:
I: Just to start us off, could you tell me different healthcare options you've heard of here in the UK?
P: Actually, mainly the GP and the NHS. Personally, I feel like the GP is probably more familiar to people. In my first year here, we were told by email and friends that we needed to register with a GP, and we all registered online. But I actually haven't used it yet. And then it’s the NHS—I see it around in real life often, like in hospitals with the big NHS signs. So, yeah, mainly these two ways.
I: Apart from school informing you by email that you needed to register with a GP, and giving you some information on healthcare, have you learnt from other sources?
P: In terms of the UK, really, just emails and maybe apps from China, like [a social platform in China]. Mostly [a social platform in China], actually.
I: Yeah, a lot of Chinese students have mentioned this app. It seems like it's really useful for a lot of people.
P: Absolutely.
I: Have you had any experiences of seeking medical help here in the UK?
P: The only experience I had was getting masks from the university. That’s probably the only direct experience I’ve had. Indirectly, though, I went with a friend to the emergency room, helped him register, waited with him, and then he got an IV drip. So, yeah, that’s indirectly related, I guess.
I: In those experiences, did you feel there was a difference between the process here in the UK and in China?
P: Overall, in terms of the steps, I feel like it’s the same — registering, paying, and waiting. But a big difference is the efficiency. It’s super slow here in the UK, while back home, it’s usually faster. So, I’d rather just take medicine myself.
I: Great. Got it. Can you remind me of how long you have been in the UK?
P: Since September 2022.
I: So over two years. During this time, have you had any infections or illnesses?
P: After coming to the UK, I got COVID. A friend recommended some medicine here, and I bought it at [high street pharmacy], though I don’t remember the name of the medicine. Yeah… I bought medicine at [high street pharmacy]. Then, in my second year, around April or May of 2024, I got some infections once. I had an allergic reaction to seafood, I think, and I broke out in hives. Those were the two main things, and then I’ve also had regular colds and fevers.
I: So you do still get colds and fevers occasionally?
P: Yes. I also have rhinitis in China. Yeah. So I often get some seasonal allergies.
I: If you have a common infection, would you consider going to a GP or handle it yourself, and why?
P: Since my infection happened after going to the ER with my friend, my first thought was that I might recover before I got my appointment. So, I searched online about what the infection could be to see what actions I could take myself to relief the symptoms, and looked up advice on various apps. I’d also ask friends for recommendations on things like ointments or syrups to try.
I: Alright. What would you hope for when you thought about getting help for common infections? 
P: Well, first, it has to be treatments to achieve quick recovery. And then, I’d hope they’d recommend something accessible with quick effects, like ointments or syrups. Something affordable, too (laughs).
I: Based on your healthcare experiences here and your views on the system, do you prefer the system here or back in China?
P: Honestly, overall, the process in China is definitely faster. But I feel like the system here encourages you to be more self-reliant. In a way, it trains you (laughs) to be independent, to learn to manage thing by yourself.
I: After these experiences, how has it trained you, and how you’ve learned to handle your illnesses?
P: Coming here from China in September 2022, I initially felt very uncertain, especially after getting COVID. I asked friends and my peer mentor for advice on how to find solutions. They told me GPs are slow, so I could try getting medicine from [high street pharmacy]. Then after going with a friend to the ER, I learned more about the process and felt more at ease dealing with it myself. I think I’ve become more rational. So by the time I had hives in my second year, I wasn’t panicking, just looked it up online, bought the medicine I needed, and handled it. I’m more relaxed about it now, not as anxious as I was at the beginning.
I: That’s great. So, do you think Chinese students face challenges or confusions about getting medical help if they are new to the UK?
P: I think the main issue is a lack of clear guidance on what to do. In my memory, I only found out how to register with a GP after I had already signed up. I actually first learned about it through my school email, but I remember that the first time I registered, it was because a friend told me about it. He wanted to register too—he’d probably seen something about it on [a social platform in China] or somewhere—and asked me to sign up together. Before we went abroad, I remember there was some kind of health coverage, kind of like insurance, that we paid for, but I didn’t really think much about it. Later, I heard that this payment went toward GP services or the NHS, and everyone said that signing up meant you could get free medical consultations and treatment. But we didn’t realize this was something we had to sign up ourselves; we thought it was already linked to something for us automatically. It’s not like you passively receive the information—you have to actively figure it out yourself. But I think for students now, like the classes of ‘24 or ‘25, it’s probably not as hard to figure out since they’re better at using social media and AI. They weren’t so common when we first got here.
I: Any advice on how they could seek help with healthcare? Such as advice for them to have a clearer understanding of the healthcare seeking process?
P: Actually, I think that if you're applying to a UK university, you could start by reaching out before you arrive—either ask your agent or email the school to learn about this stuff on your own. Yes, learn it actively. It’s about thinking of these questions ahead of time and taking the initiative to ask. Also, in my first year, the university assigned me a peer mentor. Besides academics, they’re there to help with other things too. If you have a peer mentor, you can actually ask them for help when you run into problems, like figuring out how to see a doctor. Most of them are second- or third-year students, so they usually have some experience with these things. That’s pretty much everything I can think of at the moment.
I: Good point. Ok I think we can move to our next topic on managing common infections—if you had an infection that affected your study or life, would you go to the doctor or…
P: Yes, I think I would go. I’d probably ask a friend from the same major or maybe my British roommate to come with me. The issues I’d likely be dealing with wouldn’t be anything extremely serious or life-threatening—more like something uncomfortable but manageable. I had something similar back home before, so I wouldn’t panic too much. But if it was a really severe infection, something I’d never experienced and that felt terrible, I think I’d definitely go. After all, there’s a 24-hour service for a reason, and I’d want to use it if I really needed to.
I: If a student has a bad cold and sees a GP, but the GP says it doesn’t need treatment, even if it’s affecting their studies, what kind of challenges does that pose?
P: Honestly, I think it mainly depends on how the student judges the severity of the issue based on their past experiences, either in China or from previous experiences in the UK. For me, if it’s something minor, I don’t really worry about it anymore. If the doctor tells me it’s nothing serious, I’d probably just take that answer, go home, and maybe look it up online myself, rather than becoming overly concerned about it. But if a student tends to worry more about these things, it could be different. But if it’s something that actually impacts daily life, then I think it’s best to go to the doctor for a clear answer or some specific instructions. After all, people go to the hospital to get answers, and if they don’t get what they hope for there, even if they go home and try to deal with it themselves, they won’t really know where to start. That’s when they might end up calling family back in China and cry about it. (laughs)
I: Ah yes, I got your point. Do you think your approach to handling infections here in the UK would be different from when you were in China?
P: So, I think if I had gotten sick right when I first arrived in the UK, I probably would have handled it the same way as in China—by going straight to the hospital. But the reality was that getting COVID when you arrived in the UK was pretty common, and at that time everyone knew there was a high possibility of catching it after you arrived in the UK. So, instead of going to the hospital, it was more about wearing a mask or taking strong cold medicine to get through it. That meant I didn’t even think about going to the hospital at that point. Then, after experiencing the UK hospital system—with long waiting time and long queues—it’s almost like people start to assume every visit will be a long wait, and it doesn’t seem worth the time. I think it’s really about the first impression you get when you arrive in the UK, and when you actually go to the hospital and see how things are handled, that experience definitely affects how you manage it the next time you need help.
I: Great. Earlier you said you find information online. How do you sort through it all? How do you decide what’s accurate, useful, and reliable?
P: As I remember, one time I looked something up on, uh, a website—I think it was ended with something like ‘NHS dot something,’ sort of like an official website. I thought that would be pretty reliable. And then there’s [a social platform in China]—I look at posts with a lot of likes and comments. (laughs) It’s a very practical approach!
I: (laughs) I see. Now I am going to mention some medicine names and you can tell me if you recognize any of them: amoxicillin, azithromycin, cephalexin, and levofloxacin?
P: I’ve heard of all but the last one… I think I know cephalexin. I’ve actually taken cephalexin, only when I was very sick.
I: Oh so you have taken cephalexin?
P: Yeah, I’ve taken it, but I think only twice, and only when I felt seriously awful, like I was dying. Usually, for a regular cold, I just take Sanjiu (a TCM cold granule which has antiviral and anti-inflammatory ingredients), and if it’s allergies, I just take Loratadine to relief the symptoms.
I: So, in what situation do you think you should take cephalexin?
P: I remember taking it once when I had a high fever back in China. But I’m not sure, that’s just what I remember. I haven’t taken it here in the UK.
I: Do you remember where you got the cephalexin? Was it prescribed by a doctor, or did you just buy it yourself from a pharmacy?
P: It should’ve been something my parents bought. I don’t think I ever went to the hospital to buy medicine when I was in China—my family probably had it at home. Yes.
I: Got it. Have you ever heard of antibiotics?
P: Yeah, I’ve heard of them, but I haven’t really tried them myself.
I: Do you know when antibiotics are typically used?
P: I think it’s for when a person’s heart stops... Oh wait, no, that’s adrenaline. (laughs) Antibiotics... yeah, they’re like something that boosts your immunity, right?
I: Do you know what the difference is between buying antibiotics in China and buying them in the UK?
P: (Pause)
I: It’s fine if you don’t know.
P: I think in China, they’re probably prescription-only.
I: And here in the UK?
P: I think you don’t need a prescription here.
I: So, have you learned about antibiotic resistance?
P: To be honest, I don’t know much about antibiotics. But I feel like they must interact or conflict with some other medications.
I: Great. Actually, in the UK, you need a prescription to buy antibiotics, and it’s really strictly regulated. Because antibiotics require a prescription here, and in China, they’re easier to get, so some Chinese students bring antibiotics from home. What do you think about this?
P: First of all, I definitely think it’s not a good idea. Like you said, the way antibiotics are regulated in these two countries is different, so I feel like it's kind of like... honestly, it’s like a “banned substance”. That’s how I see it. It’s not like the Sanjiu. Yeah, I don’t think it’s right... but maybe it’s just for convenience.
I: Okay. Did you bring any medicine with you?
P: I just brought Sanjiu.
I: So, if you catch a cold or have a fever, how would you handle it? Would you take the medicine you brought?
P: Yeah, I’d take Sanjiu, or maybe make some ginger tea.
I: Do you follow the instructions on the medicine, or do you just stop when you feel better?P: Actually (laughs), I’ve never looked at the instructions for any medicine. Usually, my parents just say one packet is enough, or two packets, and that’s it.
I: Okay, that’s pretty normal. So, do you think there are any issues with not following the instructions on the medicine or not taking it as prescribed by a doctor?
P: (Pause) I think, if it’s a medicine with specific instructions, or something that’s not commonly used, then yeah, it’s definitely important to… I’d definitely follow the instructions. Because the medicine’s properties, its resistance, and how it interacts with your immune system or your body can all be affected. I think it’s different from something like Sanjiu. So, those kinds of medications should definitely be taken according to the instructions. But maybe with Sanjiu, since the effect isn’t very strong or obvious, I tend to ignore the instructions.
I: So, do you think the fact that some prescription drugs are really strict here, such as antibiotics, and it’s hard to get them or for GPs to prescribe them, would affect Chinese students’ antibiotic-use behaviour?
P: I think, for example, if a student is feeling really bad, like it’s affecting their studies and daily life, but the hospital doesn’t give them a solution or just tells them to go home and figure it out, I think in that situation, something really needs to change. They should just prescribe the medication. Yes. If someone goes to the hospital and they’re already struggling or feeling like they can’t handle it, I really think the doctor should prescribe the medicine if needed. This is something that really needs to change. The process should be faster, and they shouldn’t delay giving medication—don’t let someone’s condition get worse. (laughs) It’s just not good delaying giving medication.
I: Okay, so let’s move on to the last topic. Today’s interview is actually part of my PhD project. The whole PhD is about developing an intervention to help Chinese and Indian international students in the UK with how they deal with common infections, how they better understand the healthcare system here, and how they learn to use antibiotics correctly. Since both China and India have antibiotics available over-the-counter in pharmacies, many students bring antibiotics and other medications with them. Then, when they have a cold, cough, or fever, they just take medicine themselves instead of learning how to properly handle those symptoms. What do you think of this whole plan, umm, this intervention?
P: Umm, actually (pause), when I first heard about this project, I thought, well, since it involves China and India, it makes sense because these two countries have a large number of international students here. So, if it’s a survey like this, it’ll probably show clear results. And I think there must have been cases where customs or whoever found these meds that students brought, which led to the research being done aiming at these.So, I think if this intervention really can improve things—whether it’s about Chinese or Indian students bringing meds to the UK, or if UK healthcare systems find ways to better support students with medical treatment—then I think it would be really helpful. Because (pause) I might not be the typical case—I haven’t really had the ‘I’m really sick and need to go to the hospital’ situation, but if someone really did have that, I think this kind of intervention would make a huge difference.
I: So, what kind of information do you think would be helpful to students? Specifically, for seeing a doctor and managing common infections?
P: I’d break this down into two parts: the front end and the back end. For the front end, once students pay for their healthcare insurance, it’s basically at the point when they’ve already accepted their offer and are getting ready to come to the uni. After accepting the offer, the school should, for example, within a certain number of days after payment, send out clear notices—things like how to register a GP, what not to bring, and some of the healthcare seeking processes for UK hospitals. This kind of information can all be provided to the international students who are about to head out.As for the back end… so at least the students should be informed of what they need to do. So, once they’ve been given this information, if there’s an issue at customs or if students get caught with the wrong meds, that becomes their own responsibility. But I think it’s important to have prior knowledge. As for the back end… For example, just like the career services at the university, they hold job-seeking talks every week. So you could also have NHS or GP talks every week, where students can learn about the process of seeing a doctor, how to deal with medical issues, and even some updates on medical policies. Because I’ve been to a lot of career service talks, and honestly, I think the way career services operates could be a good model for NHS and GP services to follow as well.So, yeah, I think with the front-end and back-end approach, it would definitely be better. At least, it would be better than how we were all just running around like headless chickens, trying to find information on our own through apps. Especially since Chinese students are way too dependent on [a social platform in China] the app. I think Indian students might be a bit better, but [a social platform in China] definitely has too much influence on Chinese students.
I: Right. So, besides talks and emails, what other ways do you think students could learn about information in my intervention? For example, through promotional channels?
P: Promotional channels... Actually (pauses), the Global Lounge has a WeChat account (a Chinese social app) called ‘University of Bristol Current Student’. I’m not sure who manages it, but they often post about Global Lounge updates or what’s happening around Bristol. It’s a WeChat account. Any Chinese international student who visits the Global Lounge can scan the WeChat QR code, add them as a friend, and check out their updates. Also, Career Service regularly posts about job opportunities on their website, like... this is related to career development, so they invite companies like Boss Zhipin or LinkedIn China to hold recruitment talks. I think promotion is one way. Also, strengthening partnerships with national organizations could help reach more international students. So, I think, one part is promotion, and another is collaborating with local businesses or medical institutions to co-host online or offline talks, to let students know about these issues. It might be a bit complicated, but I think it’s a long-term strategy worth considering.
I: Great, I really like the idea. I think giving talks could be very useful. It’s a good way for students to receive information.
P: Because it’s not like you can give every student a £10 voucher or something like that. It’s just not realistic if you do it among the whole uni. But rewards like this at this stage is still reasonable.
I: Great. I think the interview is almost done. Do you have any other thoughts or anything you’d like to emphasize?
P: I don’t think so. I think it’s good.

transcripts.title: Interview 03
transcripts.text:
I: First, could you tell me what you know about the different ways to get medical treatment in the UK?
P: (Laughs) I think we’re about to start another rant series. But mainly, it's the GP. However, I actually think the GP is pretty useless. For minor issues, the GP won’t treat you; they’d just refer you to [high street pharmacy], where you have to buy medicine on your own. The second scenario is when the GP thinks they can handle an illness but ends up being unable to. They start off confident, but in the end, they really can’t help. Finally, they’d send you to a specialized clinic, like an eye specialist for eye issues, or a dentist… they’d recommend private clinics. But private clinics are extremely expensive, and the GP can’t recommend any specific clinic, probably to avoid creating a commercial link. So, I end up having to check reviews on Google myself, feeling nervous about the whole thing, and it’s very costly. And as for GPs and hospitals, they’re even more useless. Usually, they’ll only refer you to a hospital if it’s something very severe. If it’s not severe enough, the GP won’t refer you to the hospital, and even when they do, it’s often ineffective. Private clinics are the most useful option, but they’re also the most expensive.
I: Right. So, if the GP can’t treat you effectively, how does that impact your work, life, or mood?
P: No, it’s not so much that it doesn’t treat me well—it’s more that it’s a huge waste of money. The GP thinks they can help, so they prescribe some medicine, and then I have to go buy it. Sometimes, there are even delays in getting the prescription, which affects treatment. If I could just go to a professional private clinic directly… But I can’t always be sure if a private clinic is actually professional. It’s a big difference compared to China, where you usually need to go to a reputable hospital and find a professional doctor, while private clinics aren’t considered very trustworthy. But here, private clinics are actually reliable and can solve the issue, but GPs can’t help. The more prescriptions the GP gives, the more money I waste. I remember some medications even went up in price.
I: Got it. Do you feel that there’s a difference between the healthcare process in the UK and in China? How different is it?
P: Yes, it’s quite different. I even think it’s the complete opposite. In China, you would generally go to the campus clinic or a proper hospital first, and private clinics are places we’d never consider or trust. But here in the UK, I don’t trust the regular GP clinics, and they’re a huge waste of money. Plus, as international students, we have to pay a hefty NHS insurance fee, which feels like a rip-off because you can’t actually use it much—even if you think you might need it, you rarely actually use it.
I: Do you go to the GP often?
P: The GP? (Sighs) I’ve been a few times, but since they couldn’t solve the issues, I ended up paying out of pocket for private clinics every time. It’s useless, but you have to register because it’s part of the healthcare process.
I: Understood. Have you ever gone to the GP for common infections?
P: Common infections… (Pauses) I think it depends on the type of infection. For example, when I first arrived, I bought the wrong shoe size, which ended up hurting my toenail. I’m not sure if that counts as an infection, but the nail eventually fell off—probably some kind of bacterial or fungal infection. The nail grew back, but part of it started growing inward into the flesh. I went to the GP for that, but it was such a hassle, so I ended up going to a private clinic to have it handled. I think that one was probably a bacterial or fungal infection, but I never fully understood what it was.
I: Do you think there are other challenges that international students face when seeking healthcare in the UK, aside from the cost?
P: Well, the cost is already a big challenge (laughs). Then there’s the challenge of finding a trustworthy clinic. Since the quality of the GP services… Can you trust their recommendations? After that, it all depends on Google. But the problem with Google is that, for things like eyeglasses stores, there are plenty of reviews and comments, so it’s easier to judge. But for other illnesses, reviews are sparse and not very reliable. The doctor at the clinic even told me that people usually only leave reviews if they’re dissatisfied, while satisfied patients rarely bother. If a clinic has only a dozen or so reviews, you can’t be sure how reliable it is, so you have to try it for yourself. And, of course, it’s expensive. So there’s always a mental burden—the high cost already adds a mental burden, plus the uncertainty. There’s also a lack of trust in the qualifications of doctors, especially when you’re new here. And with the high prices… It’s one thing if the treatment works, but what if it doesn’t? All of this creates mental pressure or even anxiety. The problem may linger, and the condition might even worsen over time. With my toenail, for example, the GP prescribed medicine, I bought it, but it didn’t work. After several attempts, they finally told me to go to a specialist. So the whole process was a waste of time and money, and it created mental stress. Yes, exactly.
I: So the whole healthcare process affects you both mentally and physically, right?
P: Yes, exactly.
I: Have you ever tried self-management, or do you have any thoughts about handling common infections on your own?
P: It depends on the type of illness. If I could handle it myself, I wouldn’t need a doctor. For a common cold or fever, I just use Lemsip or painkillers. To save money, I’ve even tried self-diagnosing… Because I couldn’t figure out what it was, I thought it might be a fungal infection, so I bought something for that. I’m no professional, and even the GP doesn’t seem to be, so we’re on the same level (laughs). In the end, I had to go to a private clinic for treatment, and they fixed it. I think colds are the most common issue here, especially when the seasons change. For that, I just buy medicine myself. I also handle minor things like coughs and other small issues on my own.
I: If you faced the same issues in China and the UK, would you handle them the same way?
P: No, in China I’d go directly to the hospital, and the treatment is quite efficient there. And in the UK, during that period—it was around the pandemic—they asked us to upload photos, and doctors would assess your condition through them. Honestly, I prefer in-person consultations. Uploading photos just doesn’t feel reliable at all.
I: Have these experiences caused you any stress?
P: A lot. The process here is different, so it’s definitely been a shock. At first, it just felt tedious, but later on, after I understood the process, I realized it’s not too bad, though I’m still not very satisfied with it.
I: When you first came to the UK, how did you learn about the healthcare options available here?
P: When we first arrived, we were all asked to register with a GP, so at first, we’d just go straight to the GP for any issues. But after having all these experiences, now I go on Xiaohongshu (a social platform in China) to check post regarding other Chinese students’ experiences. It’s really helpful in everything (laughs).
I: So you think it’s helpful to learn about these things on social media, right?
P: Yes.
I: Great. Now, let’s move on to the second topic, which is management of common infections. Have you had any common infections in the UK, and how did you deal with them?
P: Yes, I have. As for management, I think it depends on the type of infection. For example, if I accidentally cut my hand and it gets infected, I usually treat it myself, maybe with a bandage or some antiseptic spray. If it’s a bug bite that gets swollen, I’ll go to [high street pharmacy] for advice—they sometimes have effective and affordable medicine. Even though the healthcare system here isn’t great, some of their medicines work really well. For example, the medicine here for menstrual pain works much better than what I used in China—it works immediately. And for colds, Lemsip is very effective too. There are a few things here that do work well.
I: Great. Do you think Chinese students face any challenges in the UK when seeking treatment for common infections?
P: Definitely. The quality is lacking, the costs are high, official clinics aren’t helpful, and it’s hard to find official and professional clinics... I think these are common challenges for international students.
I: What do you think about Chinese students bringing their own medicine from home to the UK to handle these challenges?
P: I brought a lot of medicine myself, but I haven’t used much of it. You can’t really predict which illness you’ll get, so a lot of the medicine just expired and couldn’t be taken anymore. When preparing, you think the medicine will be useful, but it’s not actually necessary unless you have a condition that recurs frequently. Generally, people in good health with good immune system mostly just have minor symptoms such as common colds or coughs, which can be handled pretty well just by buying medicine at [high street pharmacy]. So I think bringing medicine isn’t really that necessary.
I: Alright, great. I’ll mention a few medicine names, and you can tell me if you’re familiar with them. For example, amoxicillin, cefalexin, azithromycin, gentamicin.
P: Um. I’ve heard of amoxicillin, but not the others.
I: That’s fine. Have you heard of antibiotics?
P: Yes, I’ve heard of them.
I: Do you know what antibiotics are used for?
P: I’m actually not very clear about what these medicines are for. I’ve heard the names before, but I don’t really know when they’re supposed to be used.
I: That’s okay. When you were in China, if a doctor prescribed you medicine, what would you do? For example, would you pay attention to what the medicine is and its purpose?
P: Not really. My family has a lot of healthcare professionals, so if they gave me medicine, I’d just take it. Growing up, there were only a few types of medicine I took frequently, mostly for colds or the flu. I didn’t really come across any serious illnesses.
I: Got it. Do you know the process here if you want to buy antibiotics?
P: No, I don’t.
I: That’s okay. Actually, antibiotics are used to treat bacterial infections, and here they’re prescription-only. So, like you said earlier, you need a doctor’s prescription to buy them. The medicines I just mentioned are all antibiotics. 
P: Oh I see.
I: Do you know how you’d get antibiotics in China?
P: I think you can just buy them at a pharmacy. My parents have bought them for me at a pharmacy, I think. I don’t really understand this stuff, but they do, so they’d get them from the pharmacy for me.
I: Since antibiotics are strictly regulated here in the UK, how do you feel about Chinese students bringing antibiotics from home to here?
P: I think it depends. As for medicine… If the person knows exactly what they need and how to take it—if they’re very sure of the situation… If the doctor here won’t prescribe it, there’s probably a reason or a concern for that. So, if someone brings their own, I think many students do so because of the difficulty accessing medical care, so they end up self-medicating. And many medicines might have the same ingredients in China and the UK but different names, and sometimes it’s hard to identify what illness you actually have. If students try to self-diagnose, they might confuse illnesses that have similar symptoms, unless they’re absolutely certain. Otherwise, I think it’s best not to use strictly regulated medicine on your own. Unless you have medical knowledge… And since healthcare here is difficult to access here in the UK, bringing medicine to take yourself can be very necessary and useful.
I: If a doctor prescribes you medication, do you think it’s necessary to follow the doctor’s instructions?
P: (Sighs) I think it depends. It depends on the skill level of the doctor or GP and your own knowledge. If you know more than the GP, then trust your own judgment; otherwise, go with theirs. Also, sometimes you have to compare a few opinions.
I: Got it. Let’s move on to the final topic. Actually, this interview is part of my PhD project, which involves designing an intervention to help international students from China and India understand how to manage common infections, access healthcare, and use antibiotics properly. What are your thoughts on this intervention?
P: I think it’s a good idea. But I’m not sure how you’re planning to implement it or address these issues. For example, you could get specific about which illnesses need certain treatments. P: The school website has information on registering with a GP.
I: Good. So, based on your understanding, do you think there are differences between the process of seeking healthcare in the UK compared to China?
P: I think there are some. In China, you can just go directly to the hospital and register to see a doctor immediately. But here, you can’t just go to the GP; you have to make an appointment first.
I: Which approach do you prefer?
P: I think I prefer China’s. If you’re sick, you can just go and get treated.
I: Are there other reasons you prefer the health system in China?
P: Yes, there’s also the NHS waiting list, which is really long. Even after making an appointment, you might have to wait quite a while to be seen.
I: For international students, like us Chinese students, if we get a common infection—such as an eye or ear infection, digestive issues, or respiratory infection— How would you cope with your symptoms?
P: I’m not sure about other illnesses, but if it’s a regular cold, I wouldn’t go to the GP first. I’d probably buy some over-the-counter medicine from the pharmacy. Only if it got really bad would I go to the GP.
I: So, you would choose to handle it yourself first in a way that you find feasible?
P: Yes.
I: If you thought about getting medical help, what would you expect or hope for?
P: If I had a specific condition, I’d hope the GP would refer me to a specialist.
I: Why would you want a referral to a specialist?
P: Some conditions might be beyond what the GP can treat, and they might not be able to prescribe the right medication. I think seeing a specialist would be better.
I: Right. What if the GP doesn’t refer you to a specialist? How would you feel about that?
P: (Pauses) Hmm.
I: For example, if they tell you your symptoms don’t require treatment and that you’ll recover in a few days?
P: Then I would know not to go to the GP next time for the same issue.
I: Right. You mentioned that you haven’t needed to see a doctor since arriving, but if you did try to book a GP appointment, there might be a one- or two-week wait. How would you feel if you really needed to be seen urgently but had to wait that long?
P: There wouldn’t be much I could do. From what I know, there’s another way; you can get insurance, and if you go through insurance, you don’t have to use the NHS system. This might be better if you’re often sick or urgently need to see a doctor.
I: Excellent. Do you think Chinese or other international students face particular challenges in seeking medical care in the UK?
P: I think the entire process is quite long because you need to book an appointment, then see the GP, then there’s the waiting list, and none of it is convenient. So sometimes, you might not feel like going to see the doctor right away when you’re sick.
I: Do you think there are other difficulties?
P: Also, it’s pretty expensive.
I: Right. If, due to these challenges, students bring their own medications from China to use in the UK, what are your thoughts on this practice?
P: I think I’d bring some from China too.
I: Oh really? Can you tell me why?
P: Medications might be cheaper in China, and if you urgently need a specific medicine, it might be faster to have it shipped from China instead of going through all the appointments, prescriptions, and pharmacy process here.
I: Alright. Great! Let’s move to the next topic, which is management of common infections. If you caught a common infection here, such as the eye, ear, digestive tract, or respiratory tract infections that affected your life and studies, how would you handle it?
P: If it was a bad cold, I might take some time off school, grab some cold medicine from the pharmacy, stay home, and see if I get better.
I: Do you think you would handle it differently if you were in China?
P: In China, if I had a bad cold and didn’t get better after taking medicine, I would go to the hospital, register, and get an IV drip immediately.
I: I’ll now mention a few medicine names. Let me know if you’re familiar with them: Amoxicillin, Cefalexin, Azithromycin.
P: Cefalexin seems like something you take for colds. I haven’t heard of the other two.
I: That’s alright. Are you familiar with Cefalexin?
P: I’m not sure what medicine I took when I had a cold, but the person who gave me the medicine said that it was Cefalexin.
I: Where did this happen?
P: In China. (Pauses) Probably at the hospital?
I: Not too sure? That’s fine.
P: Umm. No, I’m not very clear. In China, I don’t usually buy the medicine myself. My parents usually hand it to me and say, “Just take it.”
I: Got it. Do you normally look into what medicines you've taken or what they're supposed to treat?
P: No.
I: Right. Are you familiar with antibiotics?
P: I think I’ve heard of them.
I: Do you know what antibiotics are used for?
P: (Pauses) They’re used to kill things like viruses in your body, I think. But they also kill good cells.
I: In what situation do you think you need them?
P: I don’t think I’ve ever taken antibiotics, but I think a doctor would tell you when to take them.
I: Great. Do you know where you can get antibiotics in China?
P: I’m not sure. Maybe at the hospital or pharmacy.
I: What about in the UK?
P: The same, maybe. Either the GP prescribes it, or you get it from a pharmacy.
I: Great. If I understand correctly, you think both countries are similar when it comes to buying antibiotics?
P: Actually, I’m not sure. I think it depends on the antibiotic. In the UK, some might need a prescription, and pharmacies won’t sell them directly, but in China, you might be able to get some antibiotics without a prescription.
I: That's true. Because of management issues, in China, it's relatively easy to buy antibiotics at a pharmacy even without a prescription. But in the UK, you must have a prescription to buy antibiotics. Do you think the way prescription are regulated in the UK will affect students’ behaviour regarding antibiotic use?
P: I think it might… but I don’t get sick often. If I really need a medication urgently, or use it frequently, I could choose to bring it from China. For other conditions, like an illness I’ve never had before, I would probably go to the GP.
I: Good. Could you remind me if you brought medicine to the UK?
P: No, I didn’t bring any medicine.
I: Oh, sorry, I may have misremembered. Some students might bring antibiotics into the UK from China. What are your thoughts on this practice?
P: Since I don’t get sick often, I’m not used to taking or bringing medicine. But if people bring it, it’s probably because they get colds or illnesses often in China. They would want to have medicine with them and be prepared.
I: If they bring medicine, do you think that affects their practice to using medicine in the UK?
P: I think it depends on how serious the illness is. If someone gets sick often, they might need medicine regularly. But if they got sick, but they’re not used to self-medicating, they might not immediately start taking the medicine they brought. In this case they would rely less on their medication.
I: Great. What if they buy prescription medication but don’t follow the doctor’s instructions when taking it? What do you think about it?
P: If they don’t recover well, they can’t blame the doctor since they didn’t follow the instructions. But sometimes it's not possible to follow the doctor’s instructions exactly. For example, if a medication requires you to take it three times a day after meals, there might be times when you miss a dose or two—it’s not always manageable. But if you want to recover, it’s best to follow the instructions as closely as possible. Do what exactly the doctor says.
I: If it’s an antibiotic, what issues do you think might arise from not taking it as prescribed?
P: I think if you take too little, you won’t get better; if you take too much, it might harm your body. But I think in the UK, where antibiotics require a prescription, doctors might not prescribe a large amount at a time, so it’s not a big concern.
I: Have you heard of antibiotic resistance?
P: Yes, if you take too many, the bacteria and viruses in your body could develop resistance.
I: Okay. What do you think would happen to our health if they develop resistance? How might things change if common infections became harder to treat?
P: I think for mild cases like a common cold, resistance isn’t a huge deal because you can just take more or a higher dose, and the illness isn’t too severe. But for more serious conditions, it’s better to follow the doctor’s advice.
I: Good. I think we can move on to the next topic now. So this interview is part of my PhD project. The whole project is to develop an intervention to support international students to know how to seek medical help in the UK, how to deal with common infections by themselves, and also how to use antibiotics properly. What do you think of this project?
P: I think it’s quite good. But it needs to be visible to us; if we don’t see it, it won’t be effective or solve our issues. I think the intention is great.
I: What do you think could make it more visible?
P: Maybe the way you promote it. I know about your project through school emails, but some people don’t read emails, because we get so many each day. Emails are easily missed. I think you could make an Instagram or [a social platform in China] account. This project targets Chinese and Indian students, but it could also help students from other countries. You could also collaborate with the student union or student societies to promote it.
I: Thank you very much! If you are using it,  what would you find most helpful?
P: I saw something regarding HIV from the student union, but I’d like your content to be different—like information on flu and other common infections, and what to do in sudden situations, for example a fracture.
I: Thank you. What about information on healthcare processes here in the UK?
P: I think it should be included. Not every student will make an effort to learn how the UK healthcare system works. Also, a lot of Chinese students, especially those in one-year master’s programs, might not even consider using this healthcare system.
I: Great. I think this is the end of the interview. Is there anything else that you’d like to add that we haven’t covered, or you’d like to emphasise?
P: No. I don’t think so.
(End of recording, 26min)

transcripts.title: Interview 01
transcripts.text:
I: Just to start us off, could you tell me about different ways you can get medical help in the UK?
P: So it was just like overall two months I am here. I'm a first year PhD student. There is a hilly road. I need to walk, and this is a university accommodation. So I am living here. It's near the harbour side. OK. so and it is completely a postgraduate accommodation. The university doesn't provide any bus service for us. If our university accommodation has undergraduates and postgraduates, then they provide the universe bus service. But for us, there is no such bus for us. So I used to walk. This hilly road is so inclined. So what the feeling is sometimes my leg is painful, so and I am very new here, and I didn't register with the NHS service. So like just one week ago, I registered with the NHS service and got my NHS number, and my nearest NHS services is just here, like three to four minutes’ walk from my accommodation. It is like some GP medical services. and it is closed every day, only open on Tuesdays. So I was like, Oh my God… How … if I need some emergency, I need to go to some clinics or hospitals far away from my accommodation.For my leg pain it is now OK. I have carried my medicines from India like some calcium medicines and all. So I used to take that and used to apply the like the balm on my leg. So it is now OK. But at the moment when the pain was very increasing, I feel the worst. But regularly I need to go to university and attend all the lectures and… Like on Thursday and Friday, I have to go to the university because I am a TA of a course, so on that day I have to go to university. There is no such option to like not to go. OK, so this is the main problem I face coming here. When I was applying to NHS there is something like… some students in the WhatsApp chat group... Some students are writing that [university] is not on the list that some problems they are facing. So when I was applying there is no such way to apply from [university]. I had got my NHS number, which is normally a very long process, but I received within three to four weeks. I think that's quite like convenient. Like all of the students, everyone is applying for their NHS number, so they are quite fast let's say. But the problem is like this nearby hospital it is only Tuesday. And one more thing I want to add. I received a message from the NHS that you have to add your blood sugar level or BP something, either blood sugar or BP level, to our list like what is your patient's data or something. So I went on a Wednesday. In the Google I searched when the medical is open, when it is closed and all. So I searched in Google, it was written something but when I reached there so it…
I: Sorry I think you froze a bit. After you said you googled when it is closed, I missed the part after that, I think.
P: Yeah? Yeah, that is the last part. Yeah, that is the last. So they are completely different, like they are only open on Tuesdays and but in the Google it was written on Tuesday, Wednesday, Monday, sometimes yeah.
I: OK, apart from that, have you noticed any differences from India and here in getting medical help?
P: I saw some [a social media platform]. Whenever you are seriously sick and you call the NHS telling them like I'm very serious, but they will not pick up the call. They would tell like wait three months. But I am in a very serious condition like I am in fever, but they will then… So I I I don't know... I’ve never faced it, because I am only two months here, so I’ve never face it… but for the leg pain I face it like… It's like… before my PhD, I was in [university in India] Kanpur. Uh, I was in [university in India]. So in [university in India]  the medical system was completely different. I lived in Hall 4. From our Hall 4 to the medical service, there is only 5 to 6 minutes’ walk. Whenever we are going, we are getting the service at the time. There's no such wait. It should be like at noon, at 3:00 AM, at 4:00 AM any time.So I don't know about other… for the [university in India] specially, the medical system is very good, not like this. Because in [university in India] that is a whole campus, everything within the campus. We live, the professors live, the students live, and all the lecture hall. That's completely within a campus and everything is surrounded by a wall. But it is not like that. It's a city, and there are like the Senate houses here. Richmond building is here. Here is a fry building here, maybe other localities, the university… It is completely different. No other people without a Ucard can enter a room like in the campus. So it is completely safe here. Like after 6:00 PM is getting so dark, so we cannot get outside. But there like our life starts from 2:00 AM, everyone gets outside. So there is no such fear. No such fear of tripping your phone. No such fear of like… but here the system is not like that. And also for the medical what I'm telling, that is completely different. Here I have to call. Also there is an option for calling is my condition is so much… health type of… like I can't walk or something. The ambulance comes so fast.But I think the system in [university in India] is very much good rather than the [university] because it is not under [university], it is under Bristol, it is under UK government. It's not under like under the university, but that (in India) is under the university. It is completely definitely available for all students at [university in India] yeah. So that's my opinion. That (in India) was better. Because that is very helpful. 
One day… I had it in my hand, not in my hand, like in my armpit. I had a little… Oh, OK. One thing we have a booklet for, like a health booklet. There are doctors and all. They're all certified doctors and they used to prescribe on the booklet. OK. So on the armpit, I have a little pimple kind of… that is not a pimple. That was like a little tumour. So one day it was bleeding. It was terrifyingly bleeding, like the drops, I didn't know at the moment, like within 5 to 6 minutes, my whole surface, like my floor, completely… like it was bleeding, bleeding and bleeding. It was completely red. So it was at like 3:00 AM or 4:00 AM at night. I was completely scared. I just rushed to there. Like if it was here, so I have to first call, so then someone will come, I will go. Here the medical hall is closed at all, so I cannot go. I cannot rush to that. And even at this moment, I don't know where the medical halls are, even my flatmates are not quite familiar. But there (in India) it is 24 hours open, so anytime anyone wants to go…Like in Bristol, also there is pubs and all that runs at the midnight. Many students used to go there, especially undergrad students used to go there. If anything happens in there, someone fighting and all, maybe some has drunk so much, or some conditions get worse. So what they will do? They have to do by their own. But there (in India) you just need to call, or you just need to take them to the hospital, and then they will take care of it. They will not blame you.First, they will take care of it, then they will scold you: Why did you do that? So in India, I know that there is a scolding type of thing. We scold children. We did like, OK, my mom has scolded me. My father has scolded me… Here there is not that scolding procedure. Everyone is like no you shouldn't do that. So polite everyone here. But there, there is a culture like we scold our children.So like I somehow feel on campus medical services are very, very good for the students, yeah.
I: Oh it was not a really good experience, right? 
P: Not really. Yeah…
I: Thank you for sharing.
So you have you just been here for two months, right?
P: Two months. Yeah I arrived here on 7 November.
I: OK, so have you received any healthcare services here?
P: No, I haven't.
I: OK. If you had some common infections like eye infections or ear infections, or respiratory tract infections, would you think about getting medical help for common infections in the UK?
P: Yeah, I'll definitely think about it. Because for those I don't have… I haven't taken any medicine for that. Because I am not aware of that type of disease… I have some simple medicines like fever, cough, these medicines I have, but not have the medicines for… if I don't know about the disease, like eye infection or ear infection. I didn't face. So if I have something, if I would have something, definitely I should consult. There's no such way.
I: Yep. OK. You just mentioned that you know that you need to wait for a long time to get medical help here, right? If you can't wait that long, how would you cope with the symptoms?
P: Yeah, yeah. I think on the main road, I saw there is a big nursing home type of, so I will rush there with my flatmate. I'll go there.
I: Mm hmm. OK. If you were seeking medical help for common infections, what were you hoping for?
P: So I hope they will give me some medicines, like proper medicines, and definitely especially they will examine my eye, or what is like suitable for my… definitely not any random medicine they will give. Like please check before giving… what is suitable. Like every medicine is not suitable for everyone. So I recommend, or I will tell them please check before giving me.
I: That's really good. So you haven't been here for very long. And as an international students, what difficulties or confusion about getting medical help you had when you first arrived?
P: Yeah. Yes. So first of all, I will tell the Instagram reels should be banned. They should not scare us like that. I think like if someone call and say it is my serious injury, like my brain got damaged or my bleeding is from my brain, I think they will come. They are not so that stupid that they will not pick up the call and they will tell like wait for an hour, I don't think. But for the NHS application also, I got it… within 3-4 weeks I got my NHS number. So I think there is no such like three-months wait or four-months wait or six-months wait. I think there should be wait one or two weeks. But I think in Instagram or things online actually, they scare us more. That is not actually the scenario, what I feel. They're too much. For the content creation, they're scaring us. Maybe… There's no such thing. And maybe my nearest medical service is not a big one. That's why it is only open one day. But it is only 5-6 minutes’ walk from my accommodation. But if I go a little more like 15 minutes or 20 minutes walk, there is a big nursing home or a big hospital. So I think that is open for all the time. There should be some patients admitted all the time. I think that is more convenient. I think that is good, yeah.
I: Are there any difficulties or confusions, for international students to seek medical help in the UK?
P: For me because… No. For one thing, like I need to… what I didn't do, but I need to, I have to do, actually, I have to know the number. I just know one number that is 999. Without that number, I didn't… I didn't note down all the number. One day in our accommodation, someone smoked at night, like it was 3:30 or 3:10. Fire alarm broke out. So at the moment we were searching the fire number, we're searching the number of it, but we have to like save the number, like ambulance, police and all. I know the 999 for everything. I'll call 999. But I have to make a list in my phone. I have to save all the numbers properly. I need to do that but I didn't do. So I think not so much. And one more thing, I think you should be careful with your health. It is so windy, so always wear your hat. Always protect your throat, ears and these portions. Like if you know you have a headache… Like for me, I have a headache, like a cold wind is coming, like cutting through my head. So, I'll cover my head. Maybe I'm completely sweaty. OK, don't wear something in your jackets and all, but please cover your head, ears and throat. It will save you. So do that thing. I think like the people or the students should be a little bit conscious about their health.Don't always blame that the GP service is not good, GP service is not good… You should protect yourself first.
I: Oh, that's really great. So I think I'm going to move to the next topic, which is about management of common infections.
P: Yeah.
I: I've mentioned about eye infections and ear infections or common colds. What would you do if you have a common infection that affects your study, especially now you're doing your PhD and you have a tight schedule.
P: Like something is affecting my study… So for that, I will take the necessary steps, first of all. First of all, I will consult with the GP and all, for which like what I'm saying, for which treatments, for which diseases that I don't have medicine. I will immediately take a service from the GP, I'll consult them. If they do not pick up the call, then I'll go to the nearest hospital which is open for 24 hours. I think they should definitely do. Because coming to here, opening a bank account and all, they're quite helpful. And for medical and health is a very sensitive issue. Like for the bank and all they are serving so much, so I think for the medical also they will serve so much. I'm not giving up my hope. I'm in a quite positive hope. I hope that they will like protect their children, not just their home children, as well as the international children. I have a faith on that. For the bank and all, they are quite friendly. They're very friendly to me. Whenever at a new scenario new section is coming, I'm very polite. I'm very friendly. I love saying like: please can you do that? So like for this thing, they’d be like: OK. She's a little child. I should help her. I’ve never faced something like: No, I'll not help it. Come the next day… I’ve never faced it. So they were quite helpful. So I think for the banks and all, they are helping so much. And for the medical services, which is a more sensitive issue. They will definitely take care of us. Yeah.
I: Great. So you just said you will go to your GP and get the medication you don’t have. Would you do differently when you were in India?
P: Here, also one thing, I can do like, I will call. I will contact my parents. My parents can go to their Indian doctors like our family doctors. I will tell him or her to please check me. If they can they know me and can give me some medicines and all, then I would try to find the medicines here. If I could find them here, then I can like take that also, if the GP services’ late. So maybe this thing also I can do. If the GP service is too much late, and then I have to go to… not go to India, I have to consult the doctor in India. Then my mom will send me the medicines and all. For medicine, there is a one or two days’ courier service, so I think that also I can take. If the GP service is not working, if it is taking so much time, so then this is my next step, I will take that. Yeah, I think so.
I: Yeah. Thank you. Great! Have you heard of a medication called antibiotics?
P: Yeah. Antibiotics. Yeah, I know antibiotics.
I: Great! Do you know what they are for?
P: Antibiotics… I used to take antibiotics when, like when I'm in fever. So I used to like a paracetamol type of medicine, every six hours. I am taking paracetamol, and for… after 12 hours I'm taking antibiotic. Without antibiotic, I cannot survive. For fever, I have to take antibiotics.
I: What antibiotics do you know? Could you name some antibiotics for me?
P: I don't know…
I: Have you heard of amoxicillin, or penicillin?
P: Yeah penicillin I know. That is invented for some fever type of disease. Someone made penicillin, some scientists. Yeah, penicillin. I know.
I: Do you know that what antibiotics are for?
P: No... That is for fever or something, right? Penicillin, like, yeah, like pneumonia and all type of. Yeah. Yeah.
I: OK, so In what other situations, apart from having a fever, do you think you might need antibiotics
P: Cough, like extremely cough.
I: OK. OK.
P: Like for the dry coughs also, sometimes you need to take antibiotics. And also if we have a surgery, then also we need to take antibiotics, I think so maybe.
I: OK. OK. Do you know if there's any difference in getting antibiotics here compared to India?
P: Like here there are some prescribed medicines, and here there are some normal medicines. I don't know, if in the normal medicines… can we get the antibiotics there? But in India if we go to the store, and if we tell I need this, this, this, this, this medicines, they will give without any caution. If it is a very normal type of antibiotics and all, they don't need the prescription at all, if you go to the medical stores. But here I don't know… I don't know about the antibiotics if we take without the prescription. Maybe for antibiotics, we need the prescription, but in India we don't need. And for the antibodies for the fever and cough, we will go and say like, please give me these. They will give. Yeah.
I: OK, there are some students bring antibiotics with them when they come to the UK. What are your thoughts about this behaviour?
P: I'm also bringing antibiotics.
I: OK.
P: I have carried this much box of the medicine, this much, this much box of medicine. There are every medicine I have, like from starting from the period pain and all. Like a few years back, I had a very much pain of migraine. So for those medicines and all… like headache is complete… like even I carried 4 Otrovine… Otrovine is a nose drop. Like if our nose is got blocked or drippting, within 15 seconds, it will like clear our nose, so I carry 4 Otrovine. I have carried so much medicines, so much medicines, for whatever issues I know I have, or maybe at some point I have cough syrup, pain like body pain, head pain. There’re so many simple diseases we have throughout the year. It's not so much like… We don't go to doctor, we just need the medicine to take like vitamin specially. There's a special vitamin for me that is very good for me actually. So that is vitamin B or something. So I used to take like… there is a company that make a vitamin like… that company that medicine is very good for me so particularly.  I carried like 40 or 50 medicines, like vitamins, then calcium medicines and all. I carry so many medicines, ointment and all.
I: OK. Can I know if this is your first time studying abroad?
P: Yeah, yeah, I'm like, it is my first time. I'm. I'm outside India.
I: OK. OK. Umm. You just mentioned that you know that there are prescribed medicines here and normal medicines, right? And do you think your behaviour of medication use will be affected by this prescription thing.
P: Yeah, I think so. Yeah, I think so.
I: In what way do you think you would be affected?
P: Like some medicines I am carrying, like I don't think without the prescription they will give. There are some like pain removing medicines. We know our pain removing medicines are not good for like kidneys and all. They can damage our kidneys. So without prescriptions, I think we shouldn't get it here. I think so.
I: Great. I think we can move to the last topic. So this interview is part of my PhD project, which is to develop an intervention to support Indian and Chinese students on self-managing common infections, and also seeking healthcare here in the UK. So how do you think about this plan?
P: Yeah. I think this is very good. Because the point is where I'm raising like in India, we have a in-campus like… In the [university], if there's something like [university] Health Service that is 24 hours open for students. Please take your Ucard or if you have a booklet please take that. There are always some nurses or always someone to serve you. So that if that thing can be developed for your project it would be so great. 
Maybe within four years, I will complete my PhD and all. But after some years, like after 10 years, if there is something like that, it would be… I will be so proud of it. Like if you have done this, you have taken the initialization, and I am also the part of your project, I'd be so happy. Maybe I wouldn't get the service, but if my juniors are getting, I'd be so happy. Yeah, I think so. It'd be so good. That's why I'm very interested. Like when you are sending me the form, I don't know if I was the first or the definitely second one to fill up your form for this interview. I think like some days I’d need some data from you guys. So definitely you're there to help. Like I definitely reach out to you personally: please fill up the form. I think definitely you'll help. So I think it's completely so good and doing something for students like us. There is nothing more noble than it. Nothing.
I: Thank you. So if you were using this intervention, what information do you want to see?
P: Like the point that I'm raising, which is to have a campus-related health service for all the students for 24 hours, so we don't need to think where and when to go. So I think that would be good. Many students are facing the problem to get registration within the University site. I think university should look at that point.And for the prescribe medicine and all, every country has different scenarios. We can't expect from… Every country has different strategies. So in India, something is different. In China, something is different. In the UK, things are different. We have to respect that definitely. So if we are getting everything in India to here without the prescription, definitely they have some reasons not to give. This is not a complaint. This is what we should… we need to figure it out. OK. Yeah.
I: It's very useful. Thank you so much. Great. I think this the this is the end of the interview. And is there anything else you'd like to add or you'd like to emphasise?
P: No. Is it done?

codes.name: Severity gap
codes.definition: The participant and UK clinicians judge how serious an illness is differently.
codes.whenToUse: They feel a doctor, nurse or 111 dismissed a problem they saw as serious, or the reverse.
codes.whenNotToUse: They only describe their own symptoms without any comparison with professional judgement.
codes.example: Hypothetical: “They said it was nothing, but I could not sleep for a week.”

codes.name: Waiting & access
codes.definition: Delays, booking rules or opening hours that stop the participant getting care when they need it.
codes.whenToUse: Waiting times, appointment systems, registration delays or opening hours are a reason they did not get care.
codes.whenNotToUse: The participant chooses to wait on their own (use Enduring it).
codes.example: Hypothetical: “There were no appointments for three weeks.”

codes.name: Self-medication
codes.definition: Treating themselves without a clinician, with shop-bought medicine or medicine brought from home.
codes.whenToUse: Buying, bringing or using medicine without a prescription or advice.
codes.whenNotToUse: Taking medicine a UK clinician prescribed.
codes.example: Hypothetical: “I just took the tablets my mum packed for me.”

codes.name: Enduring it
codes.definition: Choosing to wait, rest or put up with symptoms instead of seeking care.
codes.whenToUse: They describe deciding to tolerate an illness or wait for it to pass.
codes.whenNotToUse: They wanted care but could not get it (use Waiting & access).
codes.example: Hypothetical: “I thought it would go away if I rested.”

codes.name: Comparing home system
codes.definition: Comparing UK healthcare with healthcare in their home country.
codes.whenToUse: They contrast how care, doctors, pharmacies or costs work at home and in the UK.
codes.whenNotToUse: They mention home only as where they come from, with no comparison.
codes.example: Hypothetical: “At home you just walk into a hospital.”

codes.name: Language & communication
codes.definition: Difficulty understanding or being understood by health staff.
codes.whenToUse: Language, accent, medical terms or communication style get in the way of care.
codes.whenNotToUse: General confusion about the system (use Navigating the system).
codes.example: Hypothetical: “I did not know the English word for my symptom.”

codes.name: Navigating the system
codes.definition: Knowing, or not knowing, how the UK health system works and where to go.
codes.whenToUse: Registering with a GP, using 111, A&E, walk-in centres, pharmacies, or where they got information.
codes.whenNotToUse: The barrier is waiting time once they know where to go (use Waiting & access).
codes.example: Hypothetical: “Nobody told me I had to register with a GP.”

codes.name: Antibiotic beliefs
codes.definition: Knowledge, beliefs or use of antibiotics.
codes.whenToUse: They talk about when antibiotics are needed, getting them, resistance, or bringing them from home.
codes.whenNotToUse: Other medicines that are not antibiotics (use Self-medication).
codes.example: Hypothetical: “Back home I would take antibiotics for any cold.”

You are an independent second coder for a qualitative interview study.
Apply the codebook below to each segment. A segment can have several codes or none.
Apply a code only when the segment clearly fits its definition. Words in square brackets are hidden names or places.

## Codebook
### Severity gap
Definition: The participant and UK clinicians judge how serious an illness is differently.
Use when: They feel a doctor, nurse or 111 dismissed a problem they saw as serious, or the reverse.
Do not use when: They only describe their own symptoms without any comparison with professional judgement.
Example: Hypothetical: “They said it was nothing, but I could not sleep for a week.”

### Waiting & access
Definition: Delays, booking rules or opening hours that stop the participant getting care when they need it.
Use when: Waiting times, appointment systems, registration delays or opening hours are a reason they did not get care.
Do not use when: The participant chooses to wait on their own (use Enduring it).
Example: Hypothetical: “There were no appointments for three weeks.”

### Self-medication
Definition: Treating themselves without a clinician, with shop-bought medicine or medicine brought from home.
Use when: Buying, bringing or using medicine without a prescription or advice.
Do not use when: Taking medicine a UK clinician prescribed.
Example: Hypothetical: “I just took the tablets my mum packed for me.”

### Enduring it
Definition: Choosing to wait, rest or put up with symptoms instead of seeking care.
Use when: They describe deciding to tolerate an illness or wait for it to pass.
Do not use when: They wanted care but could not get it (use Waiting & access).
Example: Hypothetical: “I thought it would go away if I rested.”

### Comparing home system
Definition: Comparing UK healthcare with healthcare in their home country.
Use when: They contrast how care, doctors, pharmacies or costs work at home and in the UK.
Do not use when: They mention home only as where they come from, with no comparison.
Example: Hypothetical: “At home you just walk into a hospital.”

### Language & communication
Definition: Difficulty understanding or being understood by health staff.
Use when: Language, accent, medical terms or communication style get in the way of care.
Do not use when: General confusion about the system (use Navigating the system).
Example: Hypothetical: “I did not know the English word for my symptom.”

### Navigating the system
Definition: Knowing, or not knowing, how the UK health system works and where to go.
Use when: Registering with a GP, using 111, A&E, walk-in centres, pharmacies, or where they got information.
Do not use when: The barrier is waiting time once they know where to go (use Waiting & access).
Example: Hypothetical: “Nobody told me I had to register with a GP.”

### Antibiotic beliefs
Definition: Knowledge, beliefs or use of antibiotics.
Use when: They talk about when antibiotics are needed, getting them, resistance, or bringing them from home.
Do not use when: Other medicines that are not antibiotics (use Self-medication).
Example: Hypothetical: “Back home I would take antibiotics for any cold.”

## Codebook
### Severity gap
Definition: The participant and UK clinicians judge how serious an illness is differently.
Use when: They feel a doctor, nurse or 111 dismissed a problem they saw as serious, or the reverse.
Do not use when: They only describe their own symptoms without any comparison with professional judgement.
Example: Hypothetical: “They said it was nothing, but I could not sleep for a week.”

### Waiting & access
Definition: Delays, booking rules or opening hours that stop the participant getting care when they need it.
Use when: Waiting times, appointment systems, registration delays or opening hours are a reason they did not get care.
Do not use when: The participant chooses to wait on their own (use Enduring it).
Example: Hypothetical: “There were no appointments for three weeks.”

### Self-medication
Definition: Treating themselves without a clinician, with shop-bought medicine or medicine brought from home.
Use when: Buying, bringing or using medicine without a prescription or advice.
Do not use when: Taking medicine a UK clinician prescribed.
Example: Hypothetical: “I just took the tablets my mum packed for me.”

### Enduring it
Definition: Choosing to wait, rest or put up with symptoms instead of seeking care.
Use when: They describe deciding to tolerate an illness or wait for it to pass.
Do not use when: They wanted care but could not get it (use Waiting & access).
Example: Hypothetical: “I thought it would go away if I rested.”

### Comparing home system
Definition: Comparing UK healthcare with healthcare in their home country.
Use when: They contrast how care, doctors, pharmacies or costs work at home and in the UK.
Do not use when: They mention home only as where they come from, with no comparison.
Example: Hypothetical: “At home you just walk into a hospital.”

### Language & communication
Definition: Difficulty understanding or being understood by health staff.
Use when: Language, accent, medical terms or communication style get in the way of care.
Do not use when: General confusion about the system (use Navigating the system).
Example: Hypothetical: “I did not know the English word for my symptom.”

### Navigating the system
Definition: Knowing, or not knowing, how the UK health system works and where to go.
Use when: Registering with a GP, using 111, A&E, walk-in centres, pharmacies, or where they got information.
Do not use when: The barrier is waiting time once they know where to go (use Waiting & access).
Example: Hypothetical: “Nobody told me I had to register with a GP.”

### Antibiotic beliefs
Definition: Knowledge, beliefs or use of antibiotics.
Use when: They talk about when antibiotics are needed, getting them, resistance, or bringing them from home.
Do not use when: Other medicines that are not antibiotics (use Self-medication).
Example: Hypothetical: “Back home I would take antibiotics for any cold.”

You are an independent second coder for a qualitative interview study.
Apply the codebook below to each segment. A segment can have several codes or none.
Apply a code only when the segment clearly fits its definition. Words in square brackets are hidden names or places.

## Codebook
### Severity gap
Definition: The participant and UK clinicians judge how serious an illness is differently.
Use when: They feel a doctor, nurse or 111 dismissed a problem they saw as serious, or the reverse.
Do not use when: They only describe their own symptoms without any comparison with professional judgement.
Example: Hypothetical: “They said it was nothing, but I could not sleep for a week.”

### Waiting & access
Definition: Delays, booking rules or opening hours that stop the participant getting care when they need it.
Use when: Waiting times, appointment systems, registration delays or opening hours are a reason they did not get care.
Do not use when: The participant chooses to wait on their own (use Enduring it).
Example: Hypothetical: “There were no appointments for three weeks.”

### Self-medication
Definition: Treating themselves without a clinician, with shop-bought medicine or medicine brought from home.
Use when: Buying, bringing or using medicine without a prescription or advice.
Do not use when: Taking medicine a UK clinician prescribed.
Example: Hypothetical: “I just took the tablets my mum packed for me.”

### Enduring it
Definition: Choosing to wait, rest or put up with symptoms instead of seeking care.
Use when: They describe deciding to tolerate an illness or wait for it to pass.
Do not use when: They wanted care but could not get it (use Waiting & access).
Example: Hypothetical: “I thought it would go away if I rested.”

### Comparing home system
Definition: Comparing UK healthcare with healthcare in their home country.
Use when: They contrast how care, doctors, pharmacies or costs work at home and in the UK.
Do not use when: They mention home only as where they come from, with no comparison.
Example: Hypothetical: “At home you just walk into a hospital.”

### Language & communication
Definition: Difficulty understanding or being understood by health staff.
Use when: Language, accent, medical terms or communication style get in the way of care.
Do not use when: General confusion about the system (use Navigating the system).
Example: Hypothetical: “I did not know the English word for my symptom.”

### Navigating the system
Definition: Knowing, or not knowing, how the UK health system works and where to go.
Use when: Registering with a GP, using 111, A&E, walk-in centres, pharmacies, or where they got information.
Do not use when: The barrier is waiting time once they know where to go (use Waiting & access).
Example: Hypothetical: “Nobody told me I had to register with a GP.”

### Antibiotic beliefs
Definition: Knowledge, beliefs or use of antibiotics.
Use when: They talk about when antibiotics are needed, getting them, resistance, or bringing them from home.
Do not use when: Other medicines that are not antibiotics (use Self-medication).
Example: Hypothetical: “Back home I would take antibiotics for any cold.”

## Segments

But yes, it was very accessible, because of the whole NHS and GP thing. Otherwise, I don't know what, I mean, it would have been way more costlier and yeah, a bit inconvenient. So this whole GP thing is, yeah, it's good. It makes it convenient for us.
[S5] (P06) I, like you asked if… There's a huge like waiting list… and if I go to a General Practitioner, and if he or she is not very thorough with the examination, what should… what will you suggest that I do.
[S6] (P06) (Pauses) No, not really. Just I need… I just needed advice because I that happened with me so…
[S7] (P06) (Pauses) I guess like if when we are filling up the online registration for the University, if they could just have like a separate section where they could mention if you have this this emergency, then even if you don’t have the NHS number, you can just go to the student health services like that, and yeah…
[S8] (P06) OK. (pauses) I'm not really. Thank you.

[S1] (P03) No, it’s not so much that it doesn’t treat me well—it’s more that it’s a huge waste of money. The GP thinks they can help, so they prescribe some medicine, and then I have to go buy it. Sometimes, there are even delays in getting the prescription, which affects treatment. If I could just go to a professional private clinic directly… But I can’t always be sure if a private clinic is actually professional. It’s a big difference compared to China, where you usually need to go to a reputable hospital and find a professional doctor, while private clinics aren’t considered very trustworthy. But here, private clinics are actually reliable and can solve the issue, but GPs can’t help. The more prescriptions the GP gives, the more money I waste. I remember some medications even went up in price.
[S2] (P03) Yes, it’s quite different. I even think it’s the complete opposite. In China, you would generally go to the campus clinic or a proper hospital first, and private clinics are places we’d never consider or trust. But here in the UK, I don’t trust the regular GP clinics, and they’re a huge waste of money. Plus, as international students, we have to pay a hefty NHS insurance fee, which feels like a rip-off because you can’t actually use it much—even if you think you might need it, you rarely actually use it.
[S3] (P03) The GP? (Sighs) I’ve been a few times, but since they couldn’t solve the issues, I ended up paying out of pocket for private clinics every time. It’s useless, but you have to register because it’s part of the healthcare process.

But for other illnesses, reviews are sparse and not very reliable. The doctor at the clinic even told me that people usually only leave reviews if they’re dissatisfied, while satisfied patients rarely bother. If a clinic has only a dozen or so reviews, you can’t be sure how reliable it is, so you have to try it for yourself. And, of course, it’s expensive. So there’s always a mental burden—the high cost already adds a mental burden, plus the uncertainty.
[S6] (P03) There’s also a lack of trust in the qualifications of doctors, especially when you’re new here. And with the high prices… It’s one thing if the treatment works, but what if it doesn’t? [S12] (P03) Yes.

[S14] (P03) Definitely. The quality is lacking, the costs are high, official clinics aren’t helpful, and it’s hard to find official and professional clinics... I think these are common challenges for international students.
